title: Are Agent Skills actually portable?
question: Can one Agent Skill work across Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Gemini CLI without client-specific forks?
verdict: Author one conservative Agent Skills core, but install and test it per host. SKILL.md, references, assets, and scripts are portable; discovery paths, invocation, consent, permissions, metadata, and distribution are not behaviorally identical.

nodes.label: Current position
nodes.text: Portable enough to author once, not portable enough to test once.

nodes.label: Shared core
nodes.text: A conservative SKILL.md package with name, description, instructions, references, assets, and scripts has a credible cross-client authoring path.

nodes.label: Open minimum
nodes.text: The Agent Skills specification defines a small required core and treats scripts, references, assets, compatibility, metadata, and allowed tools as optional layers.

nodes.label: Claude Code
nodes.text: Claude Code follows the open Agent Skills standard, discovers project and personal skills, and adds host-specific invocation, subagent, permission, and dynamic-context features.

nodes.label: Codex
nodes.text: Codex uses the open Agent Skills standard, scans .agents/skills across repository scopes, supports explicit and implicit activation, and adds optional OpenAI metadata.

nodes.label: GitHub Copilot
nodes.text: GitHub documents Agent Skills across cloud agent, code review, CLI, app, VS Code, and JetBrains, with several accepted project and personal locations.

nodes.label: Copilot run: 2/3
nodes.text: Copilot CLI 1.0.77 passed direct activation and the negative control, but its implicit run created an invalid artifact without running the requested validator or reporting a receipt.

nodes.label: Cursor
nodes.text: Cursor 2.4 added SKILL.md discovery and application in both editor and CLI, including automatic relevance matching and slash-command invocation.

nodes.label: Gemini CLI
nodes.text: Gemini CLI discovers SKILL.md packages in .gemini/skills and the .agents/skills alias, supports reload and installation commands, and asks for activation consent.

nodes.label: Paths diverge
nodes.text: The same core file is not discovered from one universal directory: native paths, aliases, scopes, precedence, and cloud behavior vary by host.

nodes.label: Behavior diverges
nodes.text: Automatic matching, explicit invocation, consent, tool pre-approval, extra frontmatter, compaction, and plugin packaging are client behaviors outside the minimal common core.

nodes.label: Ship thin adapters
nodes.text: Keep one canonical skill payload, generate or mirror only the host-specific locations and metadata, and run behavioral checks in every supported client.

nodes.label: Four clients missing
nodes.text: The shared suite now has one committed Copilot result, but Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Gemini CLI still lack comparable submitted runs.

edges.note: The standard supplies a deliberately small package contract that clients can share.
Claude Code explicitly identifies its skills as an implementation of the open standard.
Codex documents the same SKILL.md authoring model and progressive loading pattern.
Copilot adopts the standard across several GitHub and IDE surfaces.
Cursor reads SKILL.md packages in both its editor and CLI.
Gemini CLI implements the same directory-plus-SKILL.md package shape.
Claude's native .claude locations and cloud-session rules are host-specific.
Codex scans .agents locations across working-directory and repository scopes.
Copilot accepts several compatibility paths, but its supported scopes and surfaces remain product-defined.
Gemini uses a native .gemini path while accepting .agents as an alias.
Claude adds invocation control, subagent execution, dynamic context, and permission fields.
Codex adds initial-list context budgets, OpenAI metadata, and plugin distribution guidance.
Cursor defines its own automatic and slash-menu activation surfaces.
Gemini inserts an explicit consent step before a discovered skill activates.
The same skill passed explicit activation but failed the implicit artifact contract in Copilot CLI.
A shared file format does not create one universal installation or discovery location.
Portable instructions can still activate, execute, and persist differently across hosts.
One canonical payload avoids maintaining five independent instruction bodies.
Thin generated mirrors handle path differences without forking the workflow.
Per-host acceptance tests are necessary when behavior is not standardized.
The preserved implicit failure demonstrates why per-host validation must accompany a shared payload.
The shared minimum makes author-once a defensible default.
Canonical content plus thin adapters preserves portability without pretending the clients are identical.
Equivalent behavior remains an unverified hypothesis until one shared suite exercises all five clients.
